STEP 4. Common practice analysis 
There are a couple of projects being implemented in other regions of Uganda. The 
first is a small scale reforestation project in Rwoho Central Forest Reserve of the 
Nile Basin. The Rwoho project was the first ever Ugandan project to be registered 
under CDM. It is part of a project cluster of 5 similar projects aiming to provide a 
new financing mechanism to overcome the current barriers to establish timber 
plantations in Uganda and to allow communities to benefit from the CDM. In total 
the project activities cover an area of 347.1 ha within Rwoho Central Forest 
Reserve (NFA planting area: 324.9 ha (94 %), community planting area: 22.2 ha (6 
%). The Reserve covers in total an area of 9,100 ha. Based on conservative 
estimates, with a 22 years rotation cycle for all tree species, the project will 
produce 24,421 tCO2-e by 2012. The project allows the involvement of private and 
community-based tree planting initiatives with different investor shares. Due 
diligence, monitoring, validation and verification costs will be shared among the 
project cluster. Based on a successful implementation of the first pilot cluster it is 
planned to extend the portfolio across the country clustered in a number of 
deforested public forest reserves and target regions. Hence, a project design that 
can be easily replicated was developed and the concept will consider options for a 
programmatic approach. 
 
The other reforestation activity is the Community Reforestation Project in the 
Albertine Rift valley region which is currently working with established groups of

absence of the project activity (assessment and demonstration of 
additionality): 
 
The “Combined tool to identify the baseline scenario and demonstrate 
additionality in ARR CDM project activities” is used to both identify  the baseline 
scenario and to demonstrate additionally: 
 
STEP 0: Preliminary screening based on the starting date of the ARR project 
activity 
 
The proposed ARR VCS project was started in 1995 and since then, it has applied 
an externally reviewed methodology and engaged independent carbon 
monitoring experts to assess and quantify the project’s baseline scenario and net 
emissions reductions or removals resulting in carbon crediting under the SGS 
standard. In 2003 Face contracted the certification Société Générale de 
Surveillance (SGS) to validate and verify Kibale, based on SGS’ GHG Validation and 
Verification program. In the absence of an international standard defined or 
accepted by the UNFCCC Secretariat, SGS had prepared a set of criteria based on 
Decision 17/C.P7 of the Marrakech accords. These criteria act as a standard and the 
Kibale project was validated against it twice: in 2003 and 2008 respectively. 
Reports of these assessments were published in 2004 and 2009. Since then, 
project activity has been geared towards future crediting under VCS.  The 
incentive of planned sale of GHG emission allowances is evidenced in the steps 
further below of the additionality test. Without the GHG allowance sales, the 
project would not be economically attractive, and would face significant barriers.  
 
STEP 1: Identification of alternative land use scenarios to the proposed ARR VCS 
project activity 
 
Sub-step 1a: Identification of credible alternative land use scenarios to the project 
activity 
Since the lands to be planted are restricted to forestry purposes by government, 
other land uses are practically impossible, therefore the identified alternative land 
uses include three that were historically possible and one that relates to 
afforestation as recommended by the tool.

checks.question: Does the text assess the risk that stored carbon is released (reversal or non-permanence risk), for example with a risk tool, a rating or a score?

evidence.text:
1.11 Identification of risks that may substantially affect the project’s GHG 
emission reductions or removal enhancements: 
 
Non-permanence risk assessment was carried out using the VCS’  “AFOLU Non-
Permanence Risk Tool” version 3 of 8 March 2011.  According to this tool, the 
project activity was rated at a low risk after yielding a 8.5% of buffer requirement. 
The project has a system in place to identify risks and established targets to 
reduce any non-permanent risks. Procedures have been developed and 
responsibilities are well assigned with internal auditing, reviews and training in 
place.  The project also has a well qualified, experienced local management team 
in place to ensure that the project activities are implemented effectively.  The land 
planned for the project activity is wholly contained within a national park.  Based 
on the Sections 3,4 and 5 of the Uganda Wildlife Statute, the national park is fully 
owned by the government of Uganda under the UWA Act and mandated by 
Uganda Wildlife Authority on behalf of Uganda government and all Ugandans. 
Therefore, UWA has full control over the entire project lands. Additionally, the 
project will hold a 10%  VCS buffer in reserve for use in case of any loss of 
permanence.   
 
Reference is hereby made to the detailed VCS report called  “Non-Permanence Risk 
Report: Natural High Forest Rehabilitation Project on degraded land of Kibale 
National Park” for more information.   
 
 
1.12 Demonstration to confirm that the project was not implemented to 
create GHG emissions primarily for the purpose of its subsequent 
removal or destruction.  
 
 At the time the project started, in 1995, carbon credits were not a commodity and 
the concept was unheard of. Face became involved in 1994 and did not invest in 
forest destruction but in forest restoration. Instead, deforestation that took place 
in the UWA-Face project area was as a result of  encroachment by local  
communities in the period between 1970 and 1985 (Okonya, 1993). For almost  30 
years local communities were farming within the Forest Reserve, grazing cattle, 
growing maize and bananas. There was no productively managed forest in the 
area. In 1993 all inhabitants and encroachers within the boundaries of the National 
Park were were re-settled  in Kibaale District,  approximately 100 km from Kibale 
National Park (FSC, 2010; General Management Plan of Kibale National Park, 2003-
2013).  These statements are further substantiated by the Figures 1.7.1 and 1.7.2 
presented earlier in the PD. 
 
The purpose of the project is to reforest degraded lands and to promote natural 
regeneration. The project was not implemented to create GHG emissions hence 
no clearing of forest for creation of VCU’s took place.  
 
1.13 Demonstration that the project has not created another form of 
environmental credit (for example renewable energy certificates).

evidence.text:
The percentage of VCU’s to be deposited in the AFOLU Pooled buffer account is 10% = 22,172 
tCO2e (see the VCS Non-Permanence Risk Report Kibale 2017-2020 v1.0).

checks.question: Does the text describe concrete measures to monitor or prevent reversals (e.g. fire, illegal logging, land conversion)?

evidence.text:
Spot slashing: In the second year after planting, spot slashing was carried out at 
intervals of three months in the second and third year. In the fourth and fifth year, 
spot slashing was carried   at four month intervals to harden off planted crop and 
reduce maintenance costs.  
 
Spot hoeing: this was only carried out in the new crop during the second rains 
after planting. This was done in order to allow easy penetration of water and 
reduce weed competition. 
 
Fire Protection:  Fires are a major factor preventing forest regeneration. Elephant 
grass and spear grass provide excellent combustible material especially during the 
dry seasons. Planted areas are completely surrounded by a 15 m external fire line 
or by non-combustible riverine vegetation. In the centre of each 15 m firebreak 4 
m are scrapped clean of all vegetation. Furthermore, each compartment is divided 
into manageable blocks, which are separated by 10 m wide internal fire lines. 
Three meters of all internal fire lines is also scrapped clean. All fire lines are 
accessible by cars during the dry season. Training and retraining workers in fire 
fighting techniques is done. Another vital component of fire protection is fire 
awareness campaigns among the local populations neighbouring the park, 
including schools.

checks.question: Does the text show how baseline emissions are calculated, with an equation, parameter values or a numeric result?

evidence.text:
For this ARR project activity, Face in 1999 commissioned Meijer to carry out a 
baseline study whose results show that changes in the carbon stocks for both 
above and below ground biomass are expected not to exceed actual net GHG 
removals by sinks and are therefore assumed to be zero in the absence of the 
project activity. Hence the formula above is only applied to multiply the 5.2 tonnes 
of carbon per hectare (adjusted from Meijer, 1999), which is the conservative 
value of the carbon stock in the stratum ‘banana plantation’, with the combined 
area Ai of stratum ‘Planted Area’ and ‘Regenerating Area’. The total area to be 
planted during the crediting period is presented in Table 7.2 and has a size of 
6,000 hectares. In addition, the Regenerating Area is 2,593 hectares. The 
combined area is therefore 8,593 hectares. As the baseline is in a steady state, 
there is no increases in GHG removals. See Annex III for details on the estimation, 
and the spreadsheet ´ Kibale Baseline Recalculation_082711 ´, which details the 
calculation of the mean tree carbon stock in the baseline, based on inventory data 
by Meijer in 1999. In addition, the carbon stock changes in dead wood, litter and 
soil organic matter are conservatively assumed to be zero based on the 
methodology applied.

evidence.text:
6 Stakeholders comments: 
 
6.1 Brief description of how comments by local stakeholders have been 
invited and compiled: 
 
The 2006  SGS’ FSC  report states that “Community consultation was carried out at 
Kibale and all groups/individuals interviewed (e.g. the Nyabweya Parish Community, 
the Bigodi Women’s Group, the Mugume Clinic Nurse, Nursery workers) were well 
aware of the benefits of the forest, and how they could access these benefits. In 
addition, there was evidence of good communication between UWA and the 
community. Records of liaison (e.g. minutes of meetings, letters etc) were kept by 
the Assistant Warden for Community Conservation (Olivia Biira), who was appointed 
to operate in the 28 parishes, which are on the boundary of the park. UWA also 
supports the CPI (Community Protected area Institution), which comprises of people 
nominated by the communities, to represent the different Parishes and have the 
responsibility of overseeing issues in the communities, including environmental 
issues.” 
 
6.1.1 Summary of the comments received 
 
Since the start of the project activities, there have been several meetings held 
with local stakeholders. The following are only a small sample of comments 
received over the years by the UWA members of staff during community 
consultations. UWA’s Isunga office in Kibale National Park contains several folders 
where meeting minutes are filed.  
 
6.1.2 Minutes of the meeting held Mbale Parish on 17th July 1996 
 
The meeting objective was to address the community’s needs to access wild 
coffee in the National Park.  To ensure long-term sustainable harvest of wild 
coffee, community members suggested that UWA should limit the number of 
people accessing the park for coffee using distance of the village settlement from 
the park boundary and also to include those whose gardens are raided by wildlife. 
The community members further suggested that they could form community 
groups which would limit the number of people going into the park to harvest 
wild coffee. They also wanted to know if their views would be integrated into the 
coffee resource management plan.  
 
6.1.3 Workshop on management of problem animals held on July 28th 2000 at St. 
Joseph’s Inn in Virika  
 
Crop raiding by problem animals was a major issue of concern and communities 
felt that they it required joint efforts from all relevant stakeholders such as UWA 
and the Local Government to live up to their responsibilities. The major threats to 
crop damage included baboons, elephants, wild pigs, red-tailed monkeys and to a 
certain extent, birds.

evidence.text:
• collection of soil for nursery activities 
• disposal of plastic pots from seedlings 
• collection of wildlings from the forest 
 
However, from 2001 onwards seedlings raised in the communities are purchased, 
as a way of promoting further income generation activities within the local 
communities. The nursery farmers raise seedlings adjacent to the project 
nurseries not only for easy supervision by Project staff, but also for proper 
rehabilitation of areas where nursery soil is collected. Plastic pots are generally re-
used by local communities and the pots are bio-degradable. Collection of wildings 
is not considered to be on such a scale that it would have a significant impact.  
There is no road construction or harvesting activities and no chemicals or exotic 
species are being utilised. The re-establishment of natural forest is seen as a 
positive impact, enlarging the habitat for native species, protecting the park’s 
biodiversity and enhancing its tourism value. Native grasslands located in the 
project area need to be protected; they are not reforested. 
 
Detailed documentation on the analysis of environmental impacts are contained 
in the “Environmental Impact Study (EIS) report for the future operations of the 
UWA-Face Project” prepared by Environmental Monitoring Associates (EMA) Ltd 
in 1999.
